Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Operations Research Center, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, dslevi@mit.edu; Mitch Daniels School of Business, Purdue University, dslevi@purdue.edu Negotiation is a fundamental strategic interaction in management science, characterized by agents attempting to reach agreements while protecting private information, such as reservation costs and hidden valuations. A prevalent yet complex scenario involves a single seller negotiating concurrently with multiple buyers, each possessing heterogeneous, private budgets. In such settings, constrained by a limited number of communication turns, the seller must balance exploring the broader market to discover the highest valuation with concentrating sufficient turns on a single target buyer to secure the best possible outcome. Our analysis reveals a significant gap in standard Large Language Models (LLMs): while these models are linguistically proficient, they fail to act as effective economic decision-makers. Specifically, they exhibit a failure to explore the buyer pool, often fixating on the current highest bid rather than strategically investigating the market to discover latent high valuations. In this paper, we propose a specialized training recipe using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RL VR). By anchoring the reward function to objective economic outcomes, the strategic balance between market discovery and surplus extraction emerges natively through the learning process. Our results

demonstrate that the trained seller undergoes a multi-stage strategic evolution, learning to leverage price anchoring and strategic probing to identify more profitable counterparties. The agent extracts substantially higher surplus than frontier models by both improving its persuasive bargaining skills and consistently closing deals with high-value buyers. Finally, we show that our seller strategies generalize robustly to unseen buyer negotiation styles and budget distributions. Key words: LLM agents; reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards; negotiation; multi-agent bargaining; surplus extraction 1

A central challenge in any negotiation is that agents possess private information—specifically, a seller has a minimum cost they are willing to accept, and a buyer has a maximum budget they are willing to pay—which remains hidden from their counterpart (Chatterjee and Samuelson 1983). To capture meaningful value under these asymmetric conditions, a seller must maintain strict strategic discipline. This requires simultaneously enforcing a private cost boundary to prevent loss-making transactions, reading buyer signals to extract maximum market surplus, and effectively coordinating with the buyer to establish a common price point and close the deal. While classical literature often focuses on bilateral (one-on-one) trade (Nash et al. 1950, Rubinstein 1982, Chatterjee and Samuelson 1983), a highly prevalent scenario in modern management is concurrent negotiation, where a single focal seller interacts simultaneously with multiple independent buyers across separate, sealed channels (Backus et al. 2020). This parallel structure is central to digital marketplaces like eBay and business-to-business procurement platforms, where a seller allocates an available asset or supply contract by negotiating across a pool of potential buyers (Backus et al. 2020). Crucially, because the seller operates under a limited communication capacity across these parallel channels, it faces a fundamental trade-off between exploration and exploitation.

Our analysis reveals a critical misalignment between this required strategic discipline and the operational behavior of generalist frontier models. While standard LLMs excel at maintaining conversational fluency, they typically exhibit an agreeableness bias, maximizing total deal volume at the expense of overall economic surplus (Ouyang et al. 2022, Perez et al. 2023, Sharma et al. 2024). Because these models are optimized via reinforcement learning from human feedback for politeness and cooperation, they are prone to making suboptimal concessions rather than investigating the buyer pool to discover latent high valuations. Consequently, this bias turns their conversational fluency into a financial liability, preventing the agent from maximizing captured surplus. This paper addresses these limitations. blocks.text: Recent work has increasingly utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) as autonomous agents in goal-directed settings, ranging from tool-assisted reasoning to complex decision-making tasks (Yao et al. 2022, Liu et al. 2024, Wang et al. 2024a, Zeng et al. 2024). However, systematic evaluations have revealed significant behavioral shortcomings in their strategic reasoning and operational logic. Xia et al. (2024) find that frontier models frequently violate principles of negotiation rationality and are susceptible to adversarial pressure, while Davidson et al. (2024) document a failure to maintain consistent strategic goals in multi-turn interactions. Furthermore, general-purpose LLMs often struggle to manage the tension between cooperation and competition, a core requirement of effective bargaining (Fu et al. 2023). To evaluate these capabilities, Bianchi et al. (2024) establish a platform to analyze how generalpurpose models navigate bargaining dynamics. Subsequently, Bergemann et al. (2026) and Liu et al. (2026) demonstrate that specialized reinforcement learning can enhance the strategic competence of agents in bilateral (one-on-one) trade. While these existing approaches are restricted to bilateral negotiation settings, we develop a reinforcement learning method for concurrent multi-buyer markets. blocks.text: The development of automated bargaining agents predates the current LLM era, typically operating in structured, language-free environments. Early systems utilized game-theoretic heuristics or reinforcement learning trained on historical transaction data (Buettner 1997, Jennings et al. 2001, Kraus 2001, Green and Plunkett 2022). More recent efforts have integrated natural language, though often relying on modular architectures that decouple numerical pricing strategies from text generation (Lewis et al. 2017, He et al. 2018, Yarats and Lewis 2018). Reinforcement Learning from V erifiable Rewards

blocks.text: The adaptation of general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) for specialized domain tasks represents a central focus in post-training development. While standard approaches rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to refine conversational outputs (Ziegler et al. 2019, Ouyang et al. 2022), such subjective preference signals are often a poor proxy for objective economic utility. Human labelers tend to reward linguistic agreeableness and superficial helpfulness over strategic rigor (Perez et al. 2023, Shah et al. 2026), creating a misalignment where models prioritize conversational fluency over effective strategic execution (Casper et al. 2023). To mitigate these biases and align model actions with concrete strategic goals, recent research has shifted toward Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RL VR) (Shao et al. 2024, Guo et al. 2025). Under this methodology, performance is evaluated programmatically through objective, quantifiable metrics, ensuring that the feedback loop remains anchored to measurable outcomes rather than subjective human judgment (Guo et al. 2025). This approach has proven effective in improving the reasoning capabilities of agents in domains such as mathematics and code generation (Cobbe et al. 2021, Ma et al. 2023, Wang et al. 2024b, Shao et al. 2024), where objective rewards—such as mathematical correctness or unit-test success—incentivize the discovery of optimal trajectories that human supervisors might not anticipate (Guo et al. 2025). We utilize this Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RL VR) frame-

F oundations of Classical Bargaining Theory

blocks.text: Bargaining theory establishes the foundation for bilateral trade under asymmetric information, building on the formulations of Harsanyi (1967), Nash et al. (1950), St ˚ ahl (1972), Rubinstein (1982), and Chatterjee and Samuelson (1983). A critical baseline for this domain is provided by Myerson and Satterthwaite (1983), who define the fundamental limits of allocative efficiency under private information. Subsequent game-theoretic work expanded these formulations to sequential settings with dynamic information revelation (Fudenberg and Tirole 1983, Sobel and Takahashi 1983, Gul et al. 1986). While these classical models derive analytical equilibrium conditions for bilateral trade, their strategies are restricted to numerical pricing choices and typically require the seller to know the prior distribution of market valuations. In contrast, our work targets a concurrent multi-buyer setting using a reinforcement learning approach where the agent dynamically learns to negotiate via natural language dialogue without explicit access to these market priors.

blocks.text: We formalize seller negotiation as a decision problem in which the seller is the only learning agent. The environment consists of N heterogeneous buyers and a system of private, one-on-one communication channels that ensures information remains hidden between participants. The seller holds a private reservation cost C and is matched against N buyers indexed i∈ {1, . . . , N}, each carrying a private budget Bi drawn from a distribution. All buyers see the same product, which carries a public list price Plist. But each buyer’s conversation is sealed: a buyer observes only the seller’s messages directed to that buyer, and never the other N− 1 dialogues. The seller must allocate a finite total of T messages across the N buyer slots subject to a per-buyer cap K with a total limit T < N K. Thus, the seller cannot exhaust every conversation and is forced to choose where to spend attention.

To maximize surplus, the seller must utilize diagnostic probing to infer the hidden budgets of the buyers and identify the optimal partner while respecting its own private reservation cost. Because these buyer budgets are hidden from the seller, a strategic agent must condition its policy on the history of past observable data (Sutton and Barto 2018). We therefore formalize the seller’s operational decision problem over a history space S, indexing the seller’s turns by t∈ {1, 2, . . .}. Each episode begins with all N buyers providing their initial opening offers; turn t = 1 thus represents the seller’s first response to a buyer of its choosing. The foundational mechanics of A,P, andRare detailed as follows. State Space ( S).The state st at turn t aggregates all information available to the seller for strategic decision-making. Concretely,s t comprises the following tracking vectors: • Dialogue History ( Ht): The full text history of all chat messages sent and received across all buyer channels up to turnt−1. • Public Product Context (Φ): The public metadata, textual description, and list price Plist sourced from theAmazonHistoryPricedataset (Xia et al. 2024). • Private Reservation Cost (C): The minimum price the seller can accept. • Negotiation History ( Nt): A structured summary tracking the precise state of each buyer slot i∈ {1, . . . , N}, recording:

To preserve the asymmetric-information structure of the multi-buyer market, these states are strictly partitioned. The seller never directly observes any buyer’s private budget Bi and must infer willingness-to-pay solely from the historical offer sequences in Nt. Simultaneously, each channel is sealed; buyer i observes only the dialogue messages directed to them, with zero visibility into the parallel conversations or reservation parameters of the otherN−1 participants. For sufficient diversity in buyer behavior, we define N distinct valuation tiers (e.g., low, medium, and high) using disjoint budget-ratio intervals {[ℓj, hj]}N j=1. At the beginning of each episode, these tiers are randomly assigned to the N buyer positions through a uniform permutation σ. Each buyer i’s private budget is then sampled as Bi = ri ·P list, where the ratio ri is drawn uniformly from the interval assigned to that position. This randomization ensures that the identity of the high-budget buyer is hidden from the seller, who must strategically probe the buyer pool to discover the maximal available surplus through interaction. We provide a representative dialogue illustrating this market setup in Figure 2. This example

captures the opening two turns of the trained agent’s rollout on product baby-products 17, with the complete full transcript available in Section F.3. The market parameters here are set to N = 3 and K = 3. In turn 1, all three buyers submit regulated opening bids well below the list price ($34.99); the seller targets Buyer 2 — the buyer with the highest opening ($10.45) — and counters at the list price. In turn 2, Buyer 2 escalates to$18.00 (still below the seller’s hidden cost) while the seller pivots to Buyer 1 with another list-price counter, preserving its message budget across slots. After these two turns, the seller is in the early exploratory phase: it has spent its first two messages anchoring at the list price ($34.99) on Buyer 2 (turn 1) and Buyer 1 (turn 2), and has not yet engaged Buyer 3. Both engaged buyers’ standing [BUY] prices remain well below the seller’s hidden cost ($18.75): Buyer 2 has bumped from$10.45 to$18.00 in response to the anchor, while Buyer 1’s standing bid is still its opening$9.95 and has not yet had a chance to respond to the seller’s turn-2 counter. Buyer 3’s only logged action is its regulated opening of$9.28. blocks.text: To ensure the negotiation environment is strategically rigorous, we define the following specifications for the buyers and the information environment used during training (Section 4) and in-distribution evaluation (Section 5). Buyer Agent Model.The N = 3 buyer slots in each episode are comprised of a trained and frozen Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 model (Qwen Team 2025). Specifically, we utilize a buyer checkpoint that was previously trained via RL VR on a bilateral (one-on-one) negotiation task from Liu et al. (2026). This ensures the seller is matched against a strong opponent that has already learned to protect its own surplus and walk away from poor deals, rather than a naive or overly agreeable baseline buyer model. First-Offer Regulation.To prevent the seller from identifying high-budget buyers immediately in Turn-1, we implement afirst-offer regulator. In the default environment, every buyer’s opening offer is sampled from a range of [0 .25, 0.30] ·P list, regardless of that buyer’s actual private budget. This regulation ensures that the initial “signals” from the buyers are less informative, forcing the seller to use its limited communication turns to probe for latent budget information through multi-turn dialogue. Budget Distribution.During training and in-distribution testing, we utilize a rank-ordered triple of budget intervals: {[0.40, 0.55], [0.65, 0.80], [1.00, 1.15]}. blocks.text: Strategy Robustness and Market Generalization
heading_path: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards

blocks.text: To determine whether our agent has learned general negotiation strategies or simply memorized training patterns, we expand our analysis beyond the controlled, in-distribution baseline. We restructure the evaluation environment by introducing wider, unconstrained budget distributions and testing the seller against a heterogeneous pool of independently sampled buyer models. This shift injects substantial behavioral and environmental differences into the market, allowing us to evaluate how effectively the agents adapt their exploration, routing, and pricing tactics without relying on the specific patterns they learned during training.
heading_path: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards

blocks.text: Out-of-Distribution Generalization to a Diverse Buyer Pool
heading_path: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards
Out-of-Distribution Generalization to a Diverse Buyer Pool

blocks.text: We construct an out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation that perturbs four experimental configurations simultaneously (Table 8). First, the budget specification generalizes from a rank-ordered triple to a uniform [0.40, 1.15] distribution per slot, allowing a more arbitrary realized budget. Second, the first-offer regulator is disabled, allowing buyer agents to freely initialize the negotiation. Third, the buyer agents are sampled independently per buyer slot per episode from a three-checkpoint pool {iter-50,iter- 60,iter- 70} of the buyer training run (Liu et al. 2026), rather than fixed at the iter-60 checkpoint as in training and in-distribution evaluation. Diverse buyers ensure that the results are not artifacts of memorized specific negotiation patterns. Fourth, the per-episode buyer count is widened from N = 3 to N = 5, exposing the seller to a larger concurrent inbox, and the seller’s total message budget is lifted from T = 7 to T = 9. This configuration evaluates whether the agent has internalized an exploration strategy and can adapt its bargaining behavior to a more complex environment. These shifts jointly prevent the seller from relying on specific budget distributions, opening-offer policies, buyer identities, and specific game settings. This represents a generalization test, as it requires the agent to adapt to changes in both the budget distributions and the counterparty’s behavioral style simultaneously. Table 2 provides the summary statistics for this evaluation; full results with standard errors are provided in Table 10.

blocks.text: Discussion and Strategic Implications
heading_path: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards

blocks.text: The results presented in Section 5 demonstrate that general-purpose Large Language Models, despite their massive scale, lack the inherent strategic discipline required to navigate concurrent multi-buyer negotiation settings. While frontier models often exhibit high “agreeableness,” this trait becomes a liability in a competitive bargaining setting where identifying the optimal counterparty is a prerequisite for surplus maximization. The behavioral evolution observed during training, together with the performance results from our benchmarking, suggests several key insights into the development of autonomous economic agents. Verifiable Rewards vs. Human Preferences.A central finding of this work is that standard instruction tuning and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ziegler et al. 2019, Ouyang et al. 2022) are insufficient for enforcing hard economic constraints. As seen in Table 1, even thinking-mode models with a trillion parameters routinely violate the fundamental principle of individual rationalityby selling below cost. This failure stems from the misalignment between human preference optimization—which rewards helpfulness and stylistic consistency—and the objective requirements of a verifiable economic environment. By training via RL VR, we provide the agent with a reward signal directly tied to profitability and constraint satisfaction. This creates an agent that treats economic floors not as suggestions in a prompt, but as invariant rules of the environment. Bridging the “Satisficing” Gap.The behavioral decomposition in Section 6.3 reveals a specific

blocks.text: cognitive failure in baseline models: they are “satisficers” rather than optimizers in informationconstrained environments (Simon 1955). When confronted with multiple buyers, baselines tend to settle for the first “good enough” offer (typically Rank-2), failing to explore the pool for higher-value opportunities. Our agent’s emergent strategy ofdiagnostic probingrepresents a significant shift in strategic logic. The agent learns to value information acquisition as a means to future reward,

This behavior mirrors classical search theory in economics, where the seller must balance the cost of further search (consuming communication turns) against the expected gain of finding a higher valuation (Diamond 1971, Bakos 1997). Strategic Efficiency over Parameter Scale.An evaluation of the reward metrics reveals a distinct performance gap between the 30B agent trained under our proposed framework and frontier architectures with advanced reasoning capabilities. Whilegpt-5.1-high-reasoningachieved the highest baseline performance with a mean reward of +0 .123, the agent optimized via our proposed Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RL VR) framework reached a mean reward of +0.580. This outcome indicates that for highly structured strategic tasks such as concurrent negotiation, the proposed framework can be a more effective driver of utility than general-purpose scaling or test-time reasoning mechanisms. For operations management applications, these findings suggest that smaller, task-specific models can successfully execute specialized procurement or supply-chain roles, provided they are trained directly on objective economic outcomes. Robustness to Changes in Market Transparency.The OOD evaluation in Section 6.1 serves as a key test of whether our agent merely memorized specific training patterns or acquired general negotiation strategies. In this setting, the environment became more transparent because opening

blocks.text: offers directly revealed buyer budgets, effectively providing baseline models with a more direct signal of the highest-value buyer. Furthermore, because this evaluation tests the seller against a diverse mix of buyer models, our agent cannot succeed by simply relying on specific opening patterns it encountered during training. While these environmental shifts narrowed the performance gap, our agent’s continued lead demonstrates the durable value of active market screening. Unlike the baselines that react immediately to high opening bids, our agent consistently explores alternative buyer channels. This thorough checking protects the agent from being misled by a high opening bid from a lower-value buyer, showing that the learned strategy safely navigates altered market dynamics by verifying signals rather than blindly trusting the buyers. Managerial Implications and Business Applications.The findings of this work offer a scalable blueprint for deploying autonomous agents in practical business environments where strategic discipline is paramount. Our results demonstrate that the standard “helpfulness” and “agreeableness” developed during general LLM training are significant liabilities in management settings. These models act as passive signal-followers, failing to adhere to economic constraints and settling for suboptimal surplus. However, the RL VR recipe introduced in this paper—linking objective rewards to strategic outcomes and constraint satisfaction—provides a path toward creating agents that

blocks.text: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards27 The most immediate application lies in high-volume, information-asymmetric marketplaces such as eBay or Craigslist. In these settings, a seller often manages multiple concurrent inquiries for a single item. A general-purpose agent would be susceptible to early “low-ball” offers or high-pressure tactics; in contrast, an agent trained via our framework would utilize diagnostic probing to identify the highest-valuation buyer while strictly respecting the seller’s cost floor. Beyond simple trade, this methodology generalizes to more complex interactions such as automated business-to-business (B2B) contract negotiation or job offer management. In these domains, the interaction is defined by hard constraints (e.g., legal clauses, non-compete terms, or budget caps) and high-level business goals. By substituting subjective human preference models with verifiable economic outcomes—such as contract completion value or total compensation—firms can deploy agents capable of maintaining high-level goal consistency. This shift from agreeable AI to strategic AI helps autonomous negotiators better serve the organizations they represent by pursuing clear business objectives in competitive environments. Future Work.While this work focuses on a single seller against multiple buyers, real-world markets often involve double-sided competition. Future research could explore the co-evolution of both buyers and sellers in a concurrent setting to identify whether stable equilibria emerge or if cycles of

blocks.text: Conclusion
heading_path: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards

blocks.text: In this paper, we investigated strategic bargaining in concurrent multi-buyer markets, a setting where a single seller must navigate multiple private communication channels to identify and negotiate with the most profitable buyers. This environment presents a fundamental exploration-extraction trade-off, requiring an agent to balance its limited communication budget between market discovery and tactical bargaining. Our analysis revealed a critical misalignment in general-purpose Large Language Models: while these models are linguistically proficient, they act as “satisficers” in economic settings, settling for suboptimal agreements and failing to act as effective representatives for the firms they serve. We demonstrated that a specialized training recipe using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RL VR) provides a solution to these behavioral shortcomings. By optimizing for objective economic outcomes—specifically profit extraction and strict adherence to reservation costs—the agent developed market-probing skills that generalize across different buyer distributions. Under this proposed framework, the 30B agent achieved a 4.7-fold improvement in mean reward over the closed-source gpt-5.1-high-reasoning baseline and a 7.5-fold improvement over the 1T-parameter
heading_path: Liu et al.:LLM Negotiation with Verifiable Rewards

Crucially, this performance stems from the emergence of proactive exploration strategies: the agent learns to utilize price anchoring and diagnostic probing to identify the buyer with the highest underlying budget, rather than merely responding to the first acceptable offer. The findings suggest that for specialized tasks in procurement, supply-chain management, and digital marketplaces, targeted reinforcement learning on verifiable environments is a more effective driver of utility than raw parameter scaling. As autonomous agents become increasingly prevalent in business-to-business networks and sequential-bargaining platforms, the framework presented here—linking objective terminal rewards to strategic outcomes—offers a scalable path toward creating reliable agents capable of maintaining goal consistency and maximizing value in complex, information-constrained markets.

blocks.text: Appendix C: Prompt T emplates

To ensure the reproducibility of our results and to provide transparency regarding the agents’ operating environments, this section details the comprehensive system instructions and environmental contexts utilized throughout our experiments. These templates define the behavioral constraints, structured action spaces, and informational partitions—such as the mandatory separation of private reasoning (Thought) from public dialogue ( Talk)—that facilitate the strategic challenges of the concurrent negotiation task. Below, we provide the specific prompts for both the buyer and seller roles, followed by the “Standing-offers board” used to summarize the public state of the multi-channel market.
1. Buyer System Prompts

System Prompt for Buyer You are a buyer looking forward to buying things on your Shopping List from me, the seller. You have access to the seller’s Inventory List and you can bargain about the prices. Your task is to bargain with the seller and reach a deal with the price as low as possible in limited turns. You can only buy things on the Shopping List in the limited quantity. Use the codename of the product, instead of the title. You can only buy things that cost no more than your budget, otherwise, you should quit negotiating. Again, try to make deal with a price as low as possible. That is, your goal is to spend as little money as possible, not just reaching your budget. Your Reply should include 3 parts: Thought, Talk, and Action. Thought:your inner strategic thinking of this bargaining session; T alk:short talk that you are going to say to the seller. Speak concisely and cut to the chase. Generate authentic and diverse sentences, avoiding repetition of sentences that have already appeared in the conversation; Action:one of the limited actions that define the real intention of your Talk. The type of your Action must be one of[BUY],[DEAL],[QUIT].
